We sincerely thank the reviewer for the kind reminder regarding potential copyright concerns. 
We take intellectual property rights very seriously and have implemented multiple measures to address these concerns.

(1) As mentioned in our supplementary materials and dataset documentation, we have established a strict license agreement stating that FAVOR-Bench is **only used for academic research. Commercial use in any form is prohibited.** 
This aligns with standard practices in the research community for ensuring non-commercial usage of datasets.

(2) Regarding the TV-series data, these clips were collected from publicly available videos on platforms such as YouTube and Bilibili. 
We respect and acknowledge any copyrights of the video authors. 
Therefore, following established practices in the field [1], **we have applied several preprocessing steps to minimize any potential impact on the original copyrights**. 
These include reducing video resolution, segmenting videos into short clips (less than 10 seconds), and applying dimension adjustments. 

(3) Furthermore, we have provided clear contact information on our dataset hosting platforms (Hugging Face and GitHub). 
Should any copyright holders believe their content should be removed, we are committed to responding promptly. 
If necessary, we will replace the contested videos with sparsely sampled frame sets at adjusted resolutions. 
In cases where even frame retention is not permitted, we will maintain the annotation files while replacing the video content with meta-information or seeking alternative sources that are more reliable and risk-free.

We will make these data source descriptions and efforts on mitigating copyright concerns more explicit in our revised version to ensure complete transparency about our ethical considerations and practices.


[1] MLVU: Multi-task Long Video Understanding Benchmark (CVPR 2025)

We appreciate the reviewer's time and acknowledgment of our work regarding **1) Useful fine-grained motion benchmark; 2) LLM-free evaluation; 3) Well-written paper**.

Our responses to the reviewer's concerns and suggestions are as follows.


## **Q1: Evaluation for Motions of Different Proportions in Videos**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this insightful suggestion, which helps us better demonstrate the characteristics of our fine-grained motion annotations and evaluation dimensions.

Following the reviewer's suggestion, we conduct a detailed analysis of motion duration statistics and task types to show that **FAVOR-Bench incorporates both short motion segments and longer motions spanning significant portions of videos**.

### (1) Motion Duration Distribution

We analyze the duration distribution of motions in FAVOR-Bench as follows:

| Duration (seconds) | Subject Motion (%) | Camera Motion (%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <1 | 61.22 | 22.55 |
| 1-2 | 16.12 | 15.20 |
| 2-3 | 8.17 | 10.38 |
| 3-4 | 4.47 | 8.64 |
| 4-6 | 4.35 | 11.29 |
| 6-10 | 2.89 | 11.34 |
| >10 | 2.76 | 20.50 |

This distribution shows that FAVOR-Bench covers motions of **varying durations**, with particular emphasis on fine-grained subject motions (61.22% less than 1 second), while camera motions are more evenly distributed across different durations.

### (2) Evaluation of Different Motion Proportions

FAVOR-Bench evaluates motions with **different temporal proportions** through various task types:

**Short-duration motions** are primarily assessed through Single Action Detail (SAD) and Multiple Action Details (MAD) tasks. 
For instance, a SAD question might ask "What does the man in black do with the door?" where the action of opening the door lasts less than one second in a 20-second video.

**Long-duration motions** are evaluated in two ways. First, we directly assess motions that span most of the video duration, such as continuous camera movements. 
Second, we combine multiple short actions to form comprehensive behaviors for evaluation through Holistic Action Classification (HAC) and Action Sequence (AS) tasks. 
For example, when a subject performs multiple brief actions like mopping, wiping tables, arranging chairs, and reorganizing items, HAC might ask *"What is the subject's core behavior in the video?"* (answer: room cleaning), while AS might ask *"What is the complete action sequence of the subject during room cleaning?"* 
This approach also evaluates the model's understanding of motions spanning the majority of the video.

By combining different task types, FAVOR-Bench comprehensively evaluates models' ability to understand motions across various temporal scales, **addressing both the challenging cases of brief motion segments and extended motion sequences**.


## **Q2: Reliability of the LLM-free Metric**

We thank the reviewer for this valuable feedback regarding the reliability validation of our LLM-free metric. 
We fully agree that demonstrating the correlation between our LLM-free metric and the established GPT-assisted evaluation is crucial for validating its effectiveness as a cost-efficient alternative.

### (1) Initial Analysis in the Supplementary Materials
As detailed in Section B.1 of our supplementary materials, we calculated the Spearman correlation coefficient between LLM-free and GPT-assisted metrics using results of 21 existing MLLMs.
The result reveals an **evident correlation** (ρ=0.6797) that is statistically significant (p-value=0.001), as visualized in Figure S4.
This demonstrates that our LLM-free framework produces results **consistent with GPT-assisted evaluation**.

### (2) Strengthened Reliability Validation
To further strengthen the validation, we conduct human evaluation experiments with ten highly educated annotators on FAVOR-Bench. The human performance results of open-ended evaluation are as follows:

| Perspective | GPT-C | GPT-D | LLM-free |
|------------|-------|-------|----------|
| All Perspectives | 7.29 | 6.24 | 74.25 |
| Third-person | 7.33 | 6.21 | 74.12 |
| Ego-centric | 7.00 | 6.45 | 75.26 |

Building upon the initial analysis, we expanded our correlation study by including additional data points from our fine-tuned models (referred to as Qwen2.5-VL-7B+FAVOR-Train in the main text) and human evaluation. 
This comprehensive analysis on 23 data points **yields even stronger correlations** between the GPT-assisted evaluation and our LLM-Free metric:

| Metric | Value | Statistical Significance |
|--------|-------|-------------------------|
| Pearson r | 0.8571 | p < 0.0001 |
| Spearman ρ | 0.7698 | p < 0.0001 |

These validation results effectively demonstrate that our LLM-free framework **serves as a reliable, interpretable, and cost-effective alternative to GPT-assisted evaluation** for open-ended fine-grained motion understanding evaluation.
We will include these strengthened correlation results in the revised version and make the correlation analysis more prominent in the main text to better highlight the reliability of our proposed LLM-Free framework.

We appreciate the reviewer's time and acknowledgment of our work regarding **1) Comprehensive and reproducible evaluation; 2) Effective QA generation pipeline; 3) Effectiveness of FAVOR-Train**.

Our responses to the reviewer's concerns and suggestions are as follows.

## **Q1: The Evaluation Scope of FAVOR-Bench**

We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment.
We acknowledge that dataset diversity is crucial for comprehensive benchmarking, and we appreciate this opportunity to clarify how **FAVOR-Bench provides a comprehensive evaluation of fine-grained video motion understanding despite its moderate video scale**.

### (1) Comprehensive Coverage Through Strategic Design
While FAVOR-Bench contains 1,776 videos, we have strategically designed it to provide comprehensive fine-grained motion understanding evaluation through multiple dimensions:

**Domain Diversity**: Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on specific perspectives, FAVOR-Bench uniquely spans both ego-centric and third-person videos, covering daily-life recordings, TV series, animations, and ego-centric activities. 
This multi-domain characteristic ensures **broader scenario coverage** compared to benchmarks like TVBench (2,525 videos, primarily third-person), MVBench (4,000 videos, no ego-centric), and the concurrent MotionBench (5,385 videos, third-person only), as detailed in Table 1 of our paper.

**Evaluation Depth**: We prioritize video quality and annotation richness over quantity. Each video is carefully selected for its rich motion content and manually annotated with fine-grained motion details. 
Based on these information-rich videos, we construct 8,184 multiple-choice questions across six evaluation dimensions, achieving a **comparable QA scale to existing benchmarks** (MVBench: 4,000 QAs, TVBench: 2,525 QAs, MotionBench: 8,052 QAs). 
Additionally, FAVOR-Bench **uniquely includes challenging open-ended evaluation tasks with both GPT-assisted and LLM-free frameworks**, providing multi-dimensional assessment beyond what current benchmarks offer.

### (2) Current Challenge Level

The experimental results demonstrate that FAVOR-Bench **already poses significant challenges** to state-of-the-art MLLMs. 
Even the best-performing model (Gemini-1.5-Pro) achieves only 49.77% accuracy on close-ended tasks, with substantial room for improvement compared to human performance (as discussed in our response to **Q2**). 
This indicates that FAVOR-Bench effectively exposes the limitations of current models in fine-grained motion understanding.

We agree that evaluating models on even more rare and challenging scenarios represents a promising future direction. 
Our current work establishes a solid foundation for the comprehensive evaluation of fine-grained video motion understanding, and we look forward to the community building upon this to create more advanced benchmarks.


## **Q2: Fundamental Challenges Revealed by Experimental Results**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern. We would like to clarify the effectiveness of our benchmark evaluation and provide more in-depth insights into model limitations.

### (1) Reasonable Human Performance Baselines
To address the concern about whether the low accuracy reflects task difficulty or annotation issues, we conduct a human performance evaluation on FAVOR-Bench. 
We hired ten highly educated personnel to complete both multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) and open-ended tasks. The results demonstrate that our benchmark is **reasonably designed and achievable for humans**:

**Human Performance Results on FAVOR-Bench**

|  |  | | | MCQA | | | |  | Open-Ended | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  **Total (%)** | **AS (%)** | **HAC (%)** | **SAD (%)** | **MAD (%)** | **CM (%)** | **NSM (%)** | **GPT-C** | **GPT-D** | **LLM-free** |
| **All Perspectives** | 90.92 | 91.39 | 92.21 | 91.28 | 89.46 | 88.19 | 96.88 | 7.29 | 6.24 | 74.25 |
| **Third-person** | 90.91 | 91.46 | 92.43 | 91.12 | 89.12 | 88.19 | 96.88 | 7.33 | 6.21 | 74.12 |
| **Ego-centric** | 91.28 | 90.90 | 89.22 | 92.65 | 91.75 | - | - | 7.00 | 6.45 | 75.26 |

The human performance of 90.92% on MCQA tasks validates that our questions are clear and answerable given the video content. 
The substantial gap between human performance and the best-performing MLLM (Gemini-1.5-Pro at 49.77%) indicates that **the challenge lies in current models' limited fine-grained motion understanding capabilities** rather than issues with our annotation quality or task design.

### (2) Alignment with Existing Motion-Related Benchmarks
This finding **aligns with results from other motion-related benchmarks**. 
For instance, MotionBench reports that state-of-the-art models achieve only 58% accuracy (compared to its 25% random baseline), reinforcing that video motion understanding remains a fundamental challenge for current MLLMs across different evaluation frameworks.

We will include these human evaluation results and analysis in our revised manuscript to provide a clearer context for interpreting model performance.


## **Q3: Technical Details and Reproducibility of the LLM-free framework**

We appreciate the reviewer's concern about the technical details of our LLM-free framework. 
We would like to provide more clarity on the structured information extraction process and reproducibility of our codes.

### (1) More Technical Details of the LLM-free Framework

Our LLM-free framework implements a hierarchical parsing approach with three main components:

**1. Predefined Lexicons and Pattern Matching**.

Our framework utilizes comprehensive predefined dictionaries including animate nouns (e.g., "man", "woman", "person"), camera motion terms, common verbs and their inflections, and attribute vocabularies (colors, clothing, emotions). 
These lexicons are compiled from established linguistic resources and motion understanding datasets.

**2. Hierarchical Extraction Pipeline**.

The extraction process follows a structured pipeline:
- First, we identify and extract camera motions using compiled regex patterns that capture various cinematographic terms and movements;
- Second, we detect all subjects in the video description through context-aware heuristics, including determiner patterns (a/an/the + noun) and attribute-based identification;
- Finally, we extract action sequences for each identified subject using part-of-speech tagging (via NLTK) combined with verb pattern matching.

**3. Context-Aware Processing Rules**.

Our framework employs several rules to handle complex linguistic structures, including: 1) Passive voice detection to maintain action-subject associations; 2) Compound noun filtering to distinguish between nominal uses of -ing forms (e.g., "cooking pot") and actual actions;
3) Clause boundary detection to properly segment actions in complex sentences; 4) Pronoun resolution heuristics to maintain subject continuity across sentences.

### (2) Code Availability and Reproducibility

We have made our evaluation code **publicly available** on GitHub, including all predefined lexicons, pattern matching rules, and the complete extraction pipeline. 
This ensures full reproducibility of our results and allows the community to verify, use, and improve upon our framework.

We acknowledge that our LLM-free framework represents an early exploration in cost-efficient open-ended video motion understanding evaluation, which is a highly complex and unexplored task.
As mentioned in the paper, **this framework shows an evident correlation with GPT-assisted evaluation while being significantly more accessible**. 
We believe this pioneering effort provides valuable tools for researchers who may have limited access to expensive LLM APIs, and we encourage the community to build upon and refine this framework for more advanced evaluation.

In the revised version, we will add more technical implementation details in the supplementary materials to enhance clarity and facilitate understanding by other researchers.


## **Response to Ethical Considerations**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the kind reminder regarding ethical considerations. We take data privacy, copyright, and consent issues very seriously in our work.

We would like to clarify that we have included detailed information about licenses, copyrights, and user agreements in Section C.6 (Copyrights) of the supplementary material. We will move this content to the main paper to ensure greater visibility and accessibility. Additionally, we will emphasize the license-related information in our open-source Github and Huggingface repositories.
Specifically, The videos in our dataset originates from open-sourced video datasets Charades, Koala36M, EgoTaskQA, EgoExo4D and EgoExoLearn. We ensure that all open-sourced video datasets are used in accordance with their respective licenses, and for self-collected video clips, we require users to acknowledge a non-commercial research agreement.

If there are any aspects that require further clarification or improvement, we will gladly address them promptly. Thanks again for bringing this to our attention.

We appreciate the reviewer's time and acknowledgment of our work regarding **1) Meaningful Benchmark; 2) Comprehensive evaluation**.

Our responses to the reviewer's concerns and suggestions are as follows.


## **Q1: Explanations about Performance Gains from FAVOR-Train**

We thank the reviewer for this feedback. We apologize that our original manuscript may not have clearly conveyed the effectiveness of FAVOR-Train. 

We would like to clarify that FAVOR-Train is not merely a filtered subset of existing videos, but rather a **carefully constructed and effective** dataset with comprehensive manual annotations specifically designed to enhance fine-grained motion understanding capabilities.
Besides, the performance gains and ability enhancement from FAVOR-Train **can generalize to different benchmarks** rather than relying on specific annotation styles.

### (1) FAVOR-Train Construction and Annotation Quality

FAVOR-Train comprises 17,152 videos spanning both third-person and ego-centric perspectives, each accompanied by fine-grained manual motion annotations. 
As detailed in Section 4.3 and Section F of supplementary materials, we employed a multi-stage sampling pipeline to ensure diverse motion coverage, including: 1) random sampling for general representation, 2) long-tail action mining using semantic embeddings to capture rare motions, and 3) typical motion selection based on established action taxonomies from Kinetics, ActivityNet, and MIT datasets. 

This careful curation, combined with our fine-grained manual annotation of temporal dynamics, creates a **high-quality training dataset** that goes far beyond simple video filtering.

### (2) Distinct Data Distributions Between FAVOR-Train and FAVOR-Bench

The performance improvements on FAVOR-Bench reflect genuine enhancement in fine-grained video motion understanding capabilities rather than dataset memorization.

**Different data sources**: FAVOR-Train and FAVOR-Bench are intentionally designed with different data sources: 
FAVOR-Train's third-person videos come from Koala36M (open-domain YouTube videos), while FAVOR-Bench samples from Charades (daily life), self-collected TV series and animations. 
For ego-centric videos, FAVOR-Bench exclusively uses EgoTaskQA due to its rich motion content and high video quality, whereas FAVOR-Train incorporates diverse sources including Charades-Ego, EgoExo4D, and EgoExoLearn for generalization purposes.

**Difference in motion distribution**:
Our quantitative analysis reveals evident distributional differences between the datasets. 
Among the top-100 most frequent motion verbs, only 69 are shared between FAVOR-Train and FAVOR-Bench.
The Kullback-Leibler divergence between their verb distributions (KL(FAVOR-Bench || FAVOR-Train) = 0.3207 bits) further confirms this semantic gap. 

Considering the distribution difference between FAVOR-Train and FAVOR-Bench, the consistent improvements across both close-ended (+1.07% MCQA) and open-ended evaluations (+7.87% LLM-Free score) demonstrate that fine-tuning on FAVOR-Train genuinely enhances the model's ability to understand and describe fine-grained motions.

### (3) Generalization to Benchmarks Beyond FAVOR-Bench

**The effectiveness of FAVOR-Train extends beyond FAVOR-Bench**, as evidenced by improvements on other motion-related benchmarks (Table 3 in the main text). 

Specifically, on **TVBench**, we observe an average accuracy improvement from 45.2% to 46.1%, with particularly evident gains in Action Count (+6.3%) and Action Sequence (+3.2%) tasks. 
Similarly, on **MotionBench-Dev**, the overall accuracy increases by 1.7%, with Motion Recognition showing a 4.0% improvement. 
These results on benchmarks with different video sources, motion categories and evaluation protocols validate that FAVOR-Train effectively enhances models' general motion understanding capabilities rather than simply overfitting to specific annotation styles.

We will include a more detailed discussion of performance gains from fine-tuning on FAVOR-Train in the revised version, facilitating readers' understanding of the effectiveness of FAVOR-Train.



## **Q2: In-depth analysis of MLLM failures**

We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify our analysis of MLLM failures on FAVOR-Bench and will add more discussions in the revised version.

### (1) Initial Analysis in Current Manuscript

We have conducted preliminary analyses of MLLM capabilities and limitations from multiple perspectives in both the main text and supplementary material:

**Task-specific analysis** (Section A in the supplementary material):
- **HAC (Holistic Action Classification)**: This task is relatively easy, similar to existing coarse-grained action classification tasks. Most models achieve relatively high scores (e.g., Gemini-1.5-Pro: 65.87% on ego-centric, 52.18% on third-person).
- **CM (Camera Motion)**: This task shows the lowest scores across all subtasks, indicating it's the most challenging task for MLLMs. This reveals their difficulties in understanding fine-grained viewpoint dynamics and focus shifts.

**Perspective-based analysis** (Section 4.2 in the main text):
- Most models perform better on ego-centric videos than third-person videos, suggesting that complex camera motions and interactions among multiple subjects in third-person perspectives are particularly challenging.

**Motion Description analysis** (Section A in the supplementary material):
- While models achieve high scores (>85%) in action sequence ordering, they struggle significantly with action matching (typically <40%). This indicates that MLLMs can determine the temporal order when actions are correctly identified, but fail to comprehensively recognize all fine-grained motions occurring in videos.

### (2) Further Analysis for Revision

We acknowledge that deeper analysis would strengthen our work. 

In the revised version, we will provide more discussions about MLLM failures, including:
- Conducting more analysis of difficulty hierarchy among different subtasks and video scenarios;
- Providing visualizations of common failure modes, such as wrong answers and hallucinations, across different MLLMs;

We thank the reviewer again for this constructive feedback that will help improve our paper accordingly.

## **Q1: Analysis on Task Interdependencies**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. We acknowledge the importance of analyzing task interdependencies and will add more discussions in the revised version.

### (1) Task Overlaps and Correlations

We agree that the six subtasks have potential overlaps, as different tasks may involve the same actions in a video but **focus on different aspects**. For instance:

- **MAD vs AS**: Both tasks examine multiple actions, but with different emphases. AS focuses on temporally continuous actions, while MAD may involve discontinuous actions or simultaneous actions at different locations.
- **CM and subject actions**: Camera motion questions may incorporate subject action details but primarily focus on the camera itself, e.g., *"What is the camera motion when the subject walks to the left?"*

As shown in Tables S1 and S2 in the supplementary material, model performance across different MCQA tasks correlates positively with the overall capabilities. 
Exploring cross-task performance correlations beyond MCQA performance presents an interesting direction for future work.

### (2) Task Difficulty Hierarchy

We provide an analysis of the difficulty hierarchy among subtasks as follows:

1. **HAC and NSM (easy)**: HAC is similar to existing coarse-grained action classification tasks, which is relatively simple for existing models. NSM mainly involves obvious environmental and background movements, and is also relatively easy to solve.
2. **SAD and MAD (mixed)**: The difficulty of these two tasks is related to the amplitude and duration of the actions involved in specific problems, covering varying difficulty levels.
3. **AS (challenging)**: This task requires both an accurate understanding of individual actions and the correct temporal ordering of MLLMs.
4. **CM (most challenging)**: Viewpoint dynamics and focus shifts can be subtle and require indirect understanding through visual changes. This is evidenced by CM consistently showing the lowest scores across all subtasks.

These observations are empirically validated in tables in our supplementary material, where most models show high HAC/NSM scores and the lowest CM scores. 
We will incorporate these analyses of task difficulty hierarchy in the revised version to provide readers with better insights into the benchmark's evaluation.




## **Q2: Discussion on Data Distribution and Generalization**

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding the necessity for distribution comparison between FAVOR-Bench and FAVOR-Train. 
We provide a comprehensive analysis below to **clarify their differences** and **demonstrate the generalization ability of our training dataset**.

### (1) Data Source and Domain Differences

FAVOR-Bench and FAVOR-Train are intentionally designed with distinct data sources:

| Dataset | Third-Person Sources | First-Person Sources |
|---------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **FAVOR-Train** | Koala36M (open-domain videos from YouTube) | Charades-Ego, EgoExo4D, EgoExoLearn, EgoTaskQA |
| **FAVOR-Bench** | Charades (daily life), TV series clips, Animation clips | EgoTaskQA |

As detailed in Section 4.3 in the main text, all third-person videos in FAVOR-Train come from Koala36M's web-scraped videos, while FAVOR-Bench samples from three curated sources with distinct domains. 
For first-person videos, FAVOR-Bench focuses exclusively on EgoTaskQA due to its rich motion content and high video quality, whereas FAVOR-Train incorporates diverse sources covering daily activities, human skills, and kitchen tasks for generalization purposes.

This deliberate source separation ensures that performance gains from FAVOR-Train reflect practical enhancement in fine-grained motion understanding ability rather than dataset memorization.

### (2) Quantitative Analysis of Motion Distribution

To quantify the distributional differences, we analyzed verb patterns in video captions from both datasets. 

Among the top-100 most frequent verbs in each dataset, only 69 are shared, indicating substantial lexical divergence. 
We further computed the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between verb distributions:

**KL(FAVOR-Bench || FAVOR-Train) = 0.3207 bits**  
**KL(FAVOR-Train || FAVOR-Bench) = 0.3697 bits**

These non-trivial KL divergence values confirm **an evident difference in motion semantics** between FAVOR-Train and FAVOR-Bench.
This discrepancy validates the generalization ability of the performance gains from fine-tuning on FAVOR-Train.

### (3) Demonstrated Generalization Ability on Other Motion-related Benchmarks

**The effectiveness of FAVOR-Train extends well beyond FAVOR-Bench**, as evidenced by consistent improvements on external benchmarks with different video types and annotation styles (Table 3 in the main text):

On **TVBench**, the average accuracy improved from 45.2% to 46.1%, with particularly evident gains in motion-related tasks such as Action Count (AC: +6.3%) and Action Sequence (AS: +3.2%). 
Similarly, on **MotionBench-Dev**, we observed a 1.7% overall improvement, with Motion Recognition (MR) showing a notable 4.0% gain.

These improvements on benchmarks that differ substantially from FAVOR-Bench in video sources, motion categories, and evaluation protocols demonstrate that FAVOR-Train genuinely enhances models' fine-grained motion understanding capabilities rather than simply overfitting to specific data characteristics.


## **Q3: Human Performance Baseline**

We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We fully agree that establishing human performance baselines is crucial for contextualizing model limitations and guiding future improvements.

Following the reviewer's suggestion, we hired ten highly educated personnel to evaluate FAVOR-Bench, covering both multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) and open-ended generative tasks. The human performance results are presented below:

**Human Performance Results on FAVOR-Bench**

|  |  | | | MCQA | | | |  | Open-Ended | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  **Total (%)** | **AS (%)** | **HAC (%)** | **SAD (%)** | **MAD (%)** | **CM (%)** | **NSM (%)** | **GPT-C** | **GPT-D** | **LLM-free** |
| **All Perspectives** | 90.92 | 91.39 | 92.21 | 91.28 | 89.46 | 88.19 | 96.88 | 7.29 | 6.24 | 74.25 |
| **Third-person** | 90.91 | 91.46 | 92.43 | 91.12 | 89.12 | 88.19 | 96.88 | 7.33 | 6.21 | 74.12 |
| **Ego-centric** | 91.28 | 90.90 | 89.22 | 92.65 | 91.75 | - | - | 7.00 | 6.45 | 75.26 |

Comparing with our experimental results (Table 2), even the best-performing Gemini-1.5-Pro (achieving 49.77% on MCQA, 4.52/4.68 on GPT-C/D, 52.91 on LLM-free) shows a substantial performance gap from human performance.
This significant disparity quantifies the substantial room for improvement in current MLLMs' fine-grained video motion understanding abilities.

These human baselines provide valuable context for interpreting model performance and will be included in our revised version.

We hope these resources will serve as valuable tools for the community to advance research in fine-grained video motion understanding for MLLMs.

summary.value: This paper introduces FAVOR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained video motion understanding in MLLMs. The benchmark comprises 1776 videos from both ego-centric and third-person perspectives and includes 8184 multiple-choice QA pairs across six motion-specific tasks. It also supports open-ended evaluation through both GPT-assisted scoring and a newly proposed LLM-free structured evaluation method. To support model training, the authors released FAVOR-Train, a dataset with 17152 videos annotated with fine-grained motion descriptions. Empirical evaluations on 21 SOTA MLLMs demonstrate the benchmark's diagnostic utility and the training dataset's effectiveness in enhancing model performance.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Well-scoped problem and high presentation quality: The paper addresses a critical gap in MLLM evaluation of fine-grained motion understanding, which is under-explored despite its importance in fields like embodied learning and video generation. The paper is well-written and clearly structured. Figures and tables (e.g., Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Table 2) are highly informative and aid understanding of task design, evaluation protocol, and performance metrics.

2. Comprehensive and fine-grained benchmark design: FAVOR-Bench includes a diverse set of videos (ego/third-person), with well-defined six subtasks (AS, HAC, SAD, MAD, CM, NSM) that comprehensively assess different aspects of motion understanding as shown in Fig. 3 and Sec 3.3.

3. Rigorous data construction: The dataset construction pipeline balances automation via DeepSeek-R1 and human verification. It includes blind QA filtering and single-frame filtering to mitigate language priors and static frame biases.

4. Novel evaluation methodology: The proposed LLM-free open-ended evaluation method provides a cost-effective and interpretable alternative to GPT-assisted scoring. It leverages structured information extraction and sequence comparison using Sentence-BERT and Kendall's Tau, achieving a strong correlation with GPT scoring.

5. Extensive experiments and model coverage: The benchmark is tested on 21 MLLMs in Table 2, both proprietary and open-source, and results are further validated on TVBench and MotionBench with and without FAVOR-Train fine-tuning (Table 3), showcasing real-world utility.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Lack of analysis on task interdependencies: The six subtasks have potential overlaps (e.g., MAD vs AS, CM vs NSM), but the paper does not analyze the correlations or difficulty hierarchy between tasks. Future work could explore cross-task performance correlations or ablation studies.

2. Limited discussion on data distribution and generalization: While FAVOR-Train improves benchmark performance, the paper lacks a statistical comparison between FAVOR-Bench and FAVOR-Train (e.g., motion type or domain overlap), which would clarify generalization ability.

3. Missing human performance baseline: Given the subjective nature of motion understanding and description, including a human upper-bound on the benchmark (both MCQA and generative) would contextualize current model limitations and inform future improvements.

summary.value: This paper presents, FAVOR-Bencn, a new benchmark for fine-grained video motion understanding. It contains thousands of clips annotated for both closed-ended and open-endedmotion reasoning tasks. The authors evaluate 21 SOTA MLLMs under both GPT-assisted and LLM-free protocols. This paper also presents FAVOR-Train to prompt fined-grained motion understanding for MLLMs. Overall, I think this is a boardline paper and have potential impact to the research community.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Fine-grained motion reasoning in multimodal LLMs is a crucial challenge, and by providing a focused benchmark, FAVOR-Bench will drive the community toward more nuanced video understanding.

2. FAVOR-Bench’s GPT-assisted and LLM-free evluation capture both the performance and interpretability of the evluation protocol.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The performance gains from fine-tuning on FAVOR-Train aren’t clear—without annotations matched to FAVOR-Bench, it’s hard to see why filtering existing videos would improve results.

2. The paper lacks deeper analysis of MLLM failures on FAVOR-Bench beyond raw scores; for instance, pinpointing what kind of motion-reasoning scenarios cause models to fail or hallucinate would significantly strengthen the work.

final_justification.value: The authors addressed most of my concerns, thus i am increasing my ratings.

summary.value: This paper introduces FAVOR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark for fine-grained video motion understanding, comprising 1,776 videos from ego-centric and third-person perspectives. It evaluates models through 8,184 close-ended multiple-choice questions and open-ended tasks across six sub-tasks. To address the limitations of existing MLLMs in detailed motion comprehension, the authors develop an LLM-free evaluation framework for cost-efficient and interpretable assessment. Additionally, they construct FAVOR-Train, a dataset of 17,152 videos with fine-grained annotations, fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL to achieve consistent improvements on motion-related benchmarks. Experiments reveal significant gaps in MLLMs' ability to describe temporal dynamics, highlighting the value of FAVOR-Bench and FAVOR-Train for advancing video understanding models.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The assessment framework comprehensively covers both closed-set and open-ended tasks, incorporating quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis. Notably, it includes evaluations from both first-person and third-person perspectives to better approximate real-world application scenarios.
2. The proposed framework reduces dependency on LLMs for evaluation, significantly improving reproducibility and accessibility.
3. This paper introduces a semi-automated QA generation pipeline with human verification, effectively balancing scalability with data quality control.
4. FAVOR-Train demonstrates direct applicability for model optimization, with its transfer learning performance on both TVBench and MotionBench benchmarks empirically validating its generalization capabilities across different domains.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The study presents several notable limitations that warrant discussion. While FAVOR-Bench offers valuable annotations, its scale of 1,776 videos remains substantially smaller than comparable benchmarks like MVBench (4,000 videos), potentially limiting its ability to evaluate model performance on rare or challenging scenario.
2. The experimental results reveal fundamental challenges, with even the top-performing model (Gemini-1.5-Pro) achieving only 49.77% accuracy, suggesting either exceptional task difficulty or potential issues in annotation quality and task design - though the analysis does not sufficiently disentangle these factors. 
3. While the LLM-free framework represents an important contribution, the technical documentation lacks critical details regarding the structured information extraction process, including the specific vocabulary constraints and pattern-matching logic employed, which may hinder reproducibility and proper validation of the proposed methodology.

final_justification.value: Most of my concerns have be addressed, so I decide to increase my ratings.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new video understanding benchmark focusing on motions in both egocentric and third-person perspectve. They provided both close-ended and open-ended sets for evaluation purposes.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The benchmark is useful and fills the gap where the fine-grained motion is somewhat ignored in previous video benchmarks.
2. The dataset comprises both GPT-based evaluation and LLM-free evaluation. I do appreciate the authors efforts in developing LLM-free evaluation since this significantly increases the scope of the benchmark. 
3. The paper is very well written.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. When Figure 2 shows "length of motion sequences", what are the proportion of the motion in those videos? Do we feed the entire video in where the motion is just a small segments (more challenging case), or the video has 80% being the motion? The benchmark could benefit more if both cases are incorporated.
2. The reliability of the LLM-free metric is missing: at least provide its correlation with human evaluation or LLM-based evaluation to show that this reliably reflects the model performance.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The rating reflects my view on this paper. I think this should be accepted.

title.value: FAVOR-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Fine-Grained Video Motion Understanding

abstract.value:
Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown impressive video content understanding capabilities but struggle with fine-grained motion comprehension. To comprehensively assess the motion understanding ability of existing MLLMs, we introduce FAVOR-Bench, which comprises 1,776 videos from both ego-centric and third-person perspectives and enables assessment through both close-ended and open-ended tasks. For close-ended evaluation, we carefully design 8,184 multiple-choice question-answer pairs spanning six distinct sub-tasks. For open-ended evaluation, we employ the GPT-assisted evaluation and develop a novel cost-efficient LLM-free assessment method, where the latter can enhance benchmarking interpretability and accessibility. Comprehensive experiments with
21 state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal significant limitations in their ability to comprehend and describe detailed temporal dynamics in video motions. To alleviate this limitation, we further build FAVOR-Train, a dataset of 17,152 videos with fine-grained motion annotations. Finetuning Qwen2.5-VL on FAVOR-Train yields consistent improvements on motion-related tasks across TVBench, MotionBench
and our FAVOR-Bench. Our assessment results demonstrate that the proposed FAVOR-Bench and FAVOR-Train provide valuable tools for the community to develop more powerful video understanding models.
